title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM RAHAB'S PAST
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM RAHAB'S PAST
There are stories in Scripture that make us uncomfortable before they transform us.
Rahab is one of them.
Most people know her name, but few want her testimony.

Because before she became a woman of faith, before she appeared in the genealogy of Jesus Christ, before she became an example celebrated in Hebrews, Rahab carried a title that many people would never let her forget.
Prostitute.
Not widow.
Not victim.
Not misunderstood woman.
Scripture does not sanitize her past.
It records it.
And that is exactly why her story matters.
Because if God was willing to write Rahab into redemption history without erasing where she came from, perhaps He can do the same for us.
Many believers spend years trying to hide old chapters.
Old sins.
Old addictions.
Old failures.
Old scandals.
Old labels.
We quietly hope that if enough time passes, nobody will remember.
Yet Rahab's story stands in Scripture like a monument to an entirely different reality.
God does not merely cover a person's past.
He transforms it into evidence of His grace.
That lesson changed the way I see myself.
And it changed the way I see Jesus.
When we first meet Rahab in Joshua chapter 2, Israel is preparing to enter the Promised Land.
Two spies are sent into Jericho.
The city is terrified.
Rumors have spread everywhere about the God of Israel.
Kings have heard.
Armies have heard.
Entire nations have heard.
Jericho knows something is coming.
The spies eventually arrive at Rahab's house.
At first glance, this seems shocking.
Yet Scripture often reveals that God moves in places religious people rarely expect.
Rahab was not part of Israel.
She did not possess covenant privileges.
She was not raised with the Law of Moses.
She was not known for moral excellence.
Everything about her background suggested distance from God.
Yet God was already drawing her.
The Hebrew text reveals something remarkable.
Rahab tells the spies:
"I know that the LORD has given you the land."
The word translated "know" is the Hebrew word "יָדַע" (yada).
This is not a guess.
Not a possibility.
Not a rumor.
It speaks of certainty.
Conviction.
Confidence.
Somehow, while entire nations resisted God's revelation, a woman with a broken reputation recognized the truth.
That should humble all of us.
Knowledge of God is not determined by social status.
It is not determined by religious appearance.
It is not determined by public reputation.
Some people sit in churches for decades and never surrender.
Rahab heard reports and believed.
The religious world often judges from the outside.
God looks deeper.
What follows is one of the most beautiful confessions of faith in the Old Testament.
Rahab declares:
"The LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath." (Joshua 2:11)
The divine name she uses is יהוה (YHWH), the covenant name of God.
She was not merely acknowledging a powerful deity.
She was recognizing the true God.
In the middle of a pagan city.
Surrounded by idols.
Surrounded by fear.
Surrounded by darkness.
Faith was being born.
This is one reason Rahab's story continues to resonate across generations.
Many people reading this know exactly what it feels like to be surrounded by darkness while God is quietly calling them toward light.
Maybe your family does not understand your faith.
Maybe your past still follows you.
Maybe your failures seem louder than your future.
Rahab reminds us that God specializes in reaching people who appear unreachable.
The world knew Rahab for her past.
God knew her for her future.
And that difference changes everything.
The scarlet cord that hangs from Rahab's window becomes one of the most powerful images in Scripture.
The Hebrew word for scarlet is "שָׁנִי" (shani).
Its symbolism echoes throughout the biblical narrative.
When judgment came upon Jericho, Rahab and everyone sheltered under that sign were spared.
Not because they were morally superior.
Not because they earned salvation.
But because they trusted God's provision.
The parallels are impossible to ignore.
Throughout Scripture, redemption is connected to blood.
Protection is connected to God's promise.
Salvation is connected to faith.
The scarlet cord points forward.
Forward to another act of rescue.
Forward to another display of mercy.
Forward to the cross.
Centuries later, Jesus Christ would shed His blood so that sinners could be spared from judgment.
The scarlet cord hanging from Rahab's window whispers a message that reaches all the way to Calvary.
Grace is coming.
And grace has a name.
Jesus.
Then comes perhaps the most astonishing detail of all.
Rahab does not merely survive.
She is welcomed.
She becomes part of Israel.
She marries.
She builds a family.
She receives a future.
Then something happens that no human author would likely invent.
When Matthew records the genealogy of Jesus Christ, Rahab appears.
Not hidden.
Not removed.
Not edited out.
Included.
The Gospel writer intentionally preserves her place in the Messianic line.
The woman from Jericho.
The former prostitute.
The outsider.
The scandal.
Now forever connected to the lineage of the Savior.
This is where the Gospel becomes intensely personal.
Because many people believe God can forgive sins.
But they secretly doubt He can rewrite identities.
They believe He can save them.
They just do not believe He can use them.
Rahab destroys that lie.
Her story declares that God's grace is larger than your worst chapter.
Larger than your reputation.
Larger than your mistakes.
Larger than the names people have attached to you.
The Greek word often translated "grace" in the New Testament is "χάρις" (charis).
It describes unearned favor.
Undeserved kindness.
A gift that cannot be purchased.
Rahab's story is charis long before the New Testament ever uses the word.
She did not earn her place.
God gave it.
She did not deserve inclusion.
God provided it.
She did not rewrite her own story.
God did.
That is the lesson I learned from Rahab's past.
God is not intimidated by scandal.
He is not shocked by failure.
He is not limited by what people say about you.
The same God who transformed Rahab still transforms lives today.
The enemy wants people trapped in labels.
Jesus creates new creations.
The enemy wants people defined by yesterday.
Jesus speaks of redemption.
The enemy wants people convinced their story is over.
Jesus specializes in resurrection.
Some readers need to hear this today.
You are not the worst thing you have ever done.
You are not the deepest pit you have ever fallen into.
You are not the title someone attached to your name.
You are not the scandal.
You are not the failure.
If you belong to Christ, your identity is found in Him.
The Gospel does not merely improve broken people.
It makes them new.
That is why Rahab remains one of the most powerful testimonies in all of Scripture.
Her story is not ultimately about a prostitute.
It is about a Savior.
It is not about human failure.
It is about divine redemption.
It is not about what Rahab was.
It is about what Jesus would ultimately accomplish.
Maybe that is why her story feels so personal.
Because somewhere inside every believer lives a former Rahab.
A person rescued by grace.
A person who could never save themselves.
A person whose future exists only because God refused to let their past have the final word.
If this testimony stirred your heart, do not let it stop with you.
What chapter of your life are you grateful Jesus redeemed?
Your support helps expand the mission, create more faith-building content, and reach hearts that desperately need the hope of Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest miracle in Rahab's story was never that the walls fell.
It was that grace reached someone standing behind them.
